headline_findings: Because exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper feed this comparison, these findings describe those two specific papers, not Lyme disease or Long COVID in general.

Both papers show that official counting systems miss a large share of affected people - the Lyme disease paper points to a gap between a prior CDC surveillance count and a broader case-estimate, while the Long COVID paper shows a gap between self-reported symptoms and recorded diagnosis codes - but these are different kinds of undercounting measured in different units.

The Lyme disease paper quantifies out-of-pocket costs and employment loss in percentages, while the Long COVID paper quantifies quality-of-life loss in EQ-5D and QALM units; neither paper puts a dollar figure on total medical costs or productivity loss, so no direct cost comparison between the two conditions is possible from this evidence.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 43% of surveyed chronic Lyme disease respondents had more than $5,000 per year in out-of-pocket Lyme-related expenses (the Discussion section separately states 46%), versus a much smaller share of the general population.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no out-of-pocket, direct medical, or other dollar-denominated cost figures at all; its burden measures are entirely quality-of-life based.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers looking for a cost comparison between the two conditions will only find quantified out-of-pocket cost evidence on the Lyme disease side.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a 35.1 percentage-point employment-rate gap for people aged 25-54 compared with the general population, plus large shares who stopped working or reduced hours due to illness.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not measure employment or income loss directly; it mentions potential workforce impact only as a cited external implication, not as something it measured itself.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper provides its own quantified work-loss figures; the Long COVID paper flags the issue without measuring it.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 61.7% of chronic Lyme disease respondents were not diagnosed within two years of symptom onset.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not measure time-to-diagnosis or diagnostic delay at all.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic-delay evidence exists only for the Lyme disease paper, so no comparison of delay length is possible.

comparison_rows.dimension: How each condition is undercounted by official data

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper cites a gap of 270,000 cases per year between a prior CDC surveillance-reported count and a broader CDC case-ascertainment estimate, reflecting two different counting methods rather than a confidence range.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports an 18.6 percentage-point gap between people who self-reported Long COVID (24.6%) and those with a matching diagnosis code in their health record, within the same cohort.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers show that relying on official diagnosis or surveillance counts alone understates how many people are affected, even though the two papers measure this gap with completely different units and methods that should not be compared as if equivalent.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 72.3% of chronic Lyme disease respondents rated their overall health as fair or poor, versus 16.3% of the general population, alongside high rates of severe symptoms.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports a 0.22 utility-point gap on the EQ-5D-5L scale and a 0.37 QALM (quality-adjusted life-month) loss for people who self-reported Long COVID, compared with those who did not.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers document substantial, measurable declines in self-rated health or quality of life, though they use different instruments (categorical health ratings versus a standardized utility scale) that cannot be converted into one another.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states qualitatively that many insurers have adopted restrictive guidelines that may not cover extended antibiotic therapy or other treatment, without quantifying this in dollars.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper notes that patients with a low EHR-recorded diagnosis rate relative to self-report may feel unable to fully interact with primary healthcare, but this explanation is not independently measured.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers flag access-related barriers as a plausible contributor to undercounting or unmet need, but neither quantifies the barrier itself.

comparison_rows.dimension: Monetized total cost or productivity-loss figure

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper explicitly states it was not designed to calculate total medical expenditures or a dollar value for lost productivity, despite reporting utilization and cost-threshold percentages.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no direct medical, non-medical, or monetized indirect cost figures anywhere; all of its burden measures are quality-of-life based.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper can answer a total cost-of-illness question, which limits any attempt to compare the overall economic scale of the two conditions.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper relies on a self-selected, internet-recruited sample and reports only pooled figures for the full group, with no breakdown by sex, age, race, or income despite collecting some of that data.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports a single cohort-wide pooled odds ratio and disutility estimate, with no long-COVID-specific breakdown by sex, age, or ethnicity, and the cohort was 95% White, limiting ethnicity-specific analysis.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers' headline figures are averages across their whole sample, so neither can show whether burden differs across demographic subgroups.

shared_themes.theme: Official counting systems (surveillance case counts or diagnosis codes) capture substantially fewer affected people than patient self-report or broader case-ascertainment methods.

evidence.note: Reports a 270,000 cases/year gap between a prior CDC surveillance count and a broader CDC case-ascertainment estimate.
Reports an 18.6 percentage-point gap between self-reported Long COVID (24.6%) and EHR-coded diagnosis (about 6%) in the same cohort.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers document large, measurable declines in self-rated health or quality of life associated with the condition, even though they use different measurement instruments.

evidence.note: 72.3% of respondents rated their overall health as fair or poor versus 16.3% of the general population.
Self-reported Long COVID is associated with a 0.22-point lower EQ-5D-5L utility score and 0.37 more QALMs lost.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper provides a total monetized cost-of-illness or dollar-valued productivity-loss figure, despite describing substantial burden.

evidence.note: States explicitly that the study was not designed to measure total medical expenditures or calculate the economic cost of lost productivity.
Reports no direct medical, non-medical, or monetized indirect cost data anywhere in the paper.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers rely on self-selected or non-representative samples and report only pooled, whole-sample figures without demographic subgroup breakdowns.

evidence.note: Uses a self-selected, internet-recruited sample from Lyme patient forums with no sex, age, race, or income breakdown of headline figures.
Reports a single cohort-wide odds ratio and disutility estimate with no long-COVID-specific breakdown by sex, age, or ethnicity.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers point to access or coverage-related barriers as a plausible reason the condition's full impact is not captured by the formal healthcare or insurance system, though neither quantifies this barrier directly.

evidence.note: Notes that many insurers have adopted restrictive guidelines that may not cover extended treatment for chronic Lyme disease symptoms.
Suggests patients with a low EHR-recorded diagnosis rate may feel unable to fully interact with primary healthcare.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies out-of-pocket financial burden directly, showing a much higher share of patients exceeding cost thresholds than the general population.

evidence.note: 43% of respondents reported over $5,000/year in out-of-pocket Lyme-related expenses versus about 6% of the general population (the Discussion section separately states 46% vs 5%).

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies employment loss and diagnostic delay as distinct, measured burdens.

evidence.note: Reports a 35.1 percentage-point employment-rate gap for ages 25-54 and that 61.7% of respondents were not diagnosed within two years of symptom onset.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper quantifies quality-of-life loss using standardized health-utility measures and situates it alongside other serious chronic diseases.

evidence.note: Reports a 0.37 QALM loss and a 0.22-point EQ-5D-5L utility gap, with the Discussion comparing these losses to conditions such as heart failure, multiple sclerosis, and end-stage renal disease.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper provides a total monetized cost-of-illness or dollar-valued productivity-loss estimate for the condition it studies.
Neither paper disaggregates its headline burden figures by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or other demographic subgroups, despite some of that data being collected or available.
Neither paper offers a long-term or lifetime burden trajectory; both are limited to a single survey period or short follow-up window.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, so it describes what these two specific documents report, not Lyme disease or Long COVID as conditions in general. Both papers show that the condition they studied is substantially undercounted by official systems (surveillance case counts for Lyme disease, diagnosis codes for Long COVID) and that affected people experience serious declines in self-rated health or quality of life, but the two papers measure burden in very different ways - the Lyme disease paper reports percentages for out-of-pocket costs, employment loss, and diagnostic delay, while the Long COVID paper reports standardized quality-of-life utility and QALM losses. Neither paper calculates a total dollar cost of illness, so no cost comparison between the two conditions can be made from this evidence. All figures are copied directly from each paper's own key figures and should not be combined, averaged, or converted into new numbers.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison rests on a small, non-random set of papers - one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, each built from a single uploaded document - so it is not a controlled study and cannot be generalized beyond what these two documents report. Both papers carry their own stated limitations, including self-selected or non-probability samples, pooled whole-sample reporting without subgroup breakdowns, and systemic gaps in how the condition is captured by official surveillance, insurance, or diagnostic coding systems.

learning_cards.headline: Many Lyme patients waited years for diagnosis—true for Long COVID too?
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports that 61.7% of CLD respondents were not diagnosed within 2 years of symptom onset.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report a diagnostic delay or time-to-diagnosis figure.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers measure what share of self-reported cases went undiagnosed for a comparable length of time?

learning_cards.headline: Lyme patients showed a large employment gap worth checking elsewhere.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found the general-population employment rate (ages 25-54) was 35.1 percentage points higher than the CLD employment rate in the same age range.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report an employment rate figure for its cohort.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers compare employment rates between people with and without self-reported Long COVID?

learning_cards.headline: Lyme patients' out-of-pocket costs far exceeded the general population's.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found the share of CLD respondents with out-of-pocket costs above $5,000/year was 37.2 percentage points higher than the general-population share.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report an out-of-pocket spending figure.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers ask participants about out-of-pocket spending above a similar threshold?

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID patients reported sizable quality-of-life losses—worth measuring too.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found a QALM-lost difference of 0.37 QALM and an EQ-5D-5L utility gap of 0.22 points between people who self-reported Long COVID and those who did not, with an unadjusted odds ratio of 4.7 for reporting any HRQoL loss (1.46 after adjusting for breathlessness and fatigue scores).
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not report a standardized quality-of-life utility or QALM measure.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers use a standardized instrument like EQ-5D-5L to compare utility losses in people with CLD?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could gain from a standardized quality-of-life measure like the Long COVID paper uses, while the Long COVID paper could gain from tracking diagnostic delay, employment, and out-of-pocket costs the way the Lyme disease paper does.
